chapters.title: Draupadi's Swayamvara
chapters.subtitle: A great bow, a target set high, and a choice that redrew the map of kingdoms
narrative: Drupada of Panchala had not forgotten the day Drona's pupils bound him and carried him before his old schoolfellow. As the epic tells it, he performed a sacrifice to obtain a son who would kill Drona, and from the fire rose Dhrishtadyumna and then a dark, radiant daughter: Draupadi, also called Krishnaa and Yajnaseni, 'born of the sacrifice'. Drupada had always hoped to give her to Arjuna. Believing, like everyone else, that the Pandavas might have died at Varanavata, he set a test he thought only Arjuna could pass: a massive bow, and a target placed high above a mechanical device, to be struck through its opening.

Kings came from every quarter, and one after another they failed even to string the bow. Among the Brahmins in the crowd sat five brothers in disguise, newly arrived from Ekachakra with their mother. One of them rose, strung the bow in a moment and brought the target down. The princes protested that a Brahmin had carried off a kshatriya's prize; Bhima and Arjuna held them back, and Krishna, who had recognised the brothers, helped calm the quarrel.

What happened when Karna stepped forward depends on which Mahabharata you read. In the widely known vulgate text, Draupadi refuses before he can shoot, declaring she will not choose a charioteer's son. The Critical Edition prepared at Pune omits that refusal; in its text Karna does not win her either, and he is usually read as one more warrior who could not complete the feat. Which reading is older is still argued over. Popular retellings add their own details too, such as a fish target aimed at only through its reflection in water, which is not how the Critical Edition describes the contest.

At the potter's house where they lodged, the brothers called out to Kunti that they had brought home alms. Without looking, she told them to share it among themselves. Then she saw Draupadi. The marriage of one woman to five husbands troubled Drupada and, the epic admits, needed defending: Yudhishthira reasons from what he sees in his brothers' faces, and Vyasa answers with stories of Draupadi's earlier birth. A bride won by one archer became the bond tying the Pandavas to Panchala, and soon to Krishna.

story_context.when: After the escape from the house of lac and the stay at Ekachakra; the Pandavas still live disguised as Brahmins.
story_context.previously: Having freed Ekachakra from the rakshasa Baka, the Pandavas heard of Drupada's swayamvara and travelled to Panchala with Kunti.
story_context.sources_note: Karna's attempt differs by recension: the vulgate has Draupadi reject him as a suta's son, while the Critical Edition omits the rejection, leaving Karna as one more suitor who does not succeed; how much of his attempt belongs to the oldest text is debated. The fish-and-reflection target is a feature of later and regional retellings. Vyasa's justifications of the shared marriage (Draupadi's earlier life, the story of the five Indras) are part of the epic's own text, but their meaning remains much debated.

central_question.question: What does the choice of one individual mean to powerful kingdoms?
central_question.deeper_context: A swayamvara was in principle a bride's choice, yet Drupada staged it as a contest designed for one archer, and every king present understood that whoever won Draupadi also won Panchala as an ally. The outcome bound the Pandavas to Panchala and, through Krishna, to the Yadavas.

chapters.title: The Birth of Indraprastha
chapters.subtitle: A city raised from a wilderness, and the rules meant to keep it whole
narrative: News that the Pandavas lived, and were now allied to Panchala, reached Hastinapura. In Dhritarashtra's council Bhishma, Drona and Vidura urged that the brothers receive their share of the kingdom; Duryodhana wanted them weakened by intrigue, and Karna argued for open force while they were still few. Vidura was sent to bring them home, and Dhritarashtra divided the realm. The Pandavas' half was Khandavaprastha, a wild, forested tract beside the Yamuna, far from the comforts of the old capital.

There they built a city: walls and moats, gates and gardens, and a population of merchants, artisans and learned people drawn to a young king known for his fairness. They named it Indraprastha. Some later retellings credit divine architects with its building; the older narrative is more interested in what the city stood for than in how its towers rose.

The sage Narada came to warn them. He told the story of Sunda and Upasunda, asura brothers who shared everything until desire for one woman turned them against each other. The Pandavas agreed on a rule: whoever intruded on a brother alone with Draupadi would go into exile. Soon a Brahmin begged for help recovering stolen cattle, and Arjuna's weapons lay in the room where Yudhishthira sat with Draupadi. Arjuna chose the Brahmin, kept the rule against his brother's pleading, and left.

His wanderings brought him three marriages: to the Naga princess Ulupi, to Chitrangada of Manipura, and to Subhadra, Krishna's sister, whom he carried off on Krishna's own advice while Balarama raged. Subhadra arrived at Indraprastha dressed as a cowherd woman to greet Draupadi, and in time bore Abhimanyu. The kingdom flourished. But on its edge the Khandava forest still stood, and it had inhabitants of its own.

story_context.when: After the marriage at Panchala: the Pandavas return to Hastinapura, receive half the kingdom and found Indraprastha.
story_context.previously: The swayamvara revealed that the Pandavas had survived Varanavata, and their alliance with Panchala made them impossible to ignore.
story_context.sources_note: The length of Arjuna's exile (traditionally twelve years) and how his marriages fit a vow of celibacy were discussed by commentators; the text has Ulupi argue that saving her life outweighs the vow. Divine builders of Indraprastha appear mainly in later and regional retellings.

central_question.question: Can a new kingdom escape the conflicts of its past?
central_question.deeper_context: Dhritarashtra's partition was meant to end the rivalry by giving the Pandavas a realm of their own, but the land they received was a wilderness, and the grievances of Varanavata went with both sides.

chapters.title: The Burning of Khandava
chapters.subtitle: Gifts of fire, and grudges that outlive a generation
narrative: Krishna and Arjuna had gone to the banks of the Yamuna near Indraprastha when a tall Brahmin, blazing like the sun, came to ask them for food. He was Agni, the fire god, and the food he wanted was the Khandava forest. He had tried before to consume it, but Indra protected the forest for the sake of his friend Takshaka, the Naga who lived there, and put out every attempt with rain. To make the heroes equal to Indra, Agni asked Varuna for gifts: Arjuna received the bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot bearing a monkey banner; Krishna received a discus, given in the text by Agni himself, and from Varuna the mace Kaumodaki.

The epic describes the burning without softening it. Krishna and Arjuna drove round the forest on two sides while it burned, and turned back the creatures that tried to escape. When Indra's clouds gathered, Arjuna's arrows formed a canopy that held off the rain, and the gods who came to fight eventually withdrew, told by a voice that Takshaka was not even in the forest. Many modern readers find the episode troubling, and some read it as a memory of land being cleared for farming. Those readings are interpretations; the text presents it as a heroic feat that pleased Agni.

A few survived. Maya, an asura architect, ran to Arjuna for protection, and Krishna lowered his discus; in gratitude Maya would build the Pandavas an assembly hall like no other. Takshaka's son Ashvasena escaped. The Nagas come back at decisive moments: Ashvasena seeks Arjuna at Kurukshetra, and Takshaka, the forest's absent lord, later causes the death of Arjuna's grandson Parikshit. That death leads Janamejaya to the snake sacrifice where the Mahabharata is first recited.

story_context.when: The closing episode of the Adi Parva, after Arjuna's return with Subhadra and the birth of Abhimanyu.
story_context.previously: Indraprastha flourishes, but the Khandava forest still stands at its edge, protected by Indra for the Naga Takshaka.
story_context.sources_note: The episode is in the Critical Edition and closes the Adi Parva. Explanations of Agni's illness, the number of his failed attempts and the lists of creatures vary between manuscripts and retellings. Ecological and land-clearing readings are modern interpretations. Takshaka's killing of Parikshit is set off in the text by a sage's curse, so the link back to Khandava is thematic rather than a stated motive.

central_question.question: Who pays for the founding of a city?
central_question.deeper_context: The burning cleared the land beside Indraprastha and armed its heroes, but the forest's inhabitants were given no say, and the text itself records their attempts to flee.

chapters.title: The Rajasuya Assembly
chapters.subtitle: A king of kings is consecrated, and the first honour starts a quarrel
narrative: Maya kept his word and built the Pandavas an assembly hall full of illusions: pools that looked like solid floor, crystal floors that looked like water. In it the sage Narada described the halls of the gods and brought a message from Pandu, who wished his son to perform the Rajasuya, the royal consecration that proclaims one king paramount over others. Yudhishthira turned to Krishna, and Krishna named the obstacle: Jarasandha of Magadha, who held many captive kings he meant to sacrifice, and whose attacks had already driven the Yadavas from Mathura to Dwaraka.

Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna entered Jarasandha's capital, Girivraja, dressed as snataka Brahmins, and challenged him to single combat. Jarasandha chose Bhima. The text has them wrestle for nearly two weeks before Bhima killed him, and the captive kings were freed and Jarasandha's son placed on the throne. Then the four younger brothers went out in the four directions, conquering or securing the submission of kingdoms and bringing back tribute.

At the sacrifice, with Vyasa among the officiating priests, Bhishma advised that the first honour go to Krishna, and Sahadeva offered it. Shishupala of Chedi refused to accept this: Krishna was not a king, he said, and the Pandavas had insulted every ruler present. His abuse grew. Bhishma told how Krishna had promised Shishupala's mother to forgive him a hundred offences, and when that limit was passed Krishna released his discus. The epic says that a radiance rose from the fallen king and entered Krishna.

Duryodhana stayed on after the guests left and walked through Maya's hall. He mistook a crystal floor for a pool, and then a real pool for floor and fell in, and Bhima laughed, and the attendants with him. In popular retellings Draupadi mocks him as 'the blind man's son'; that line is not found in the Critical Edition, though Duryodhana's sense of humiliation and envy is central there. He went home burning, with Shakuni at his side.

story_context.sources_note: Draupadi's taunt 'the son of a blind man is blind' is a later popular addition and is not in the Critical Edition, where Bhima and the servants are the ones shown laughing at Duryodhana; who joins the laughter varies between versions. The length of the Jarasandha duel, the number of captive kings and the lists of kingdoms in the digvijaya vary by manuscript. The radiance entering Krishna is read devotionally (as liberation) and also critically.

chapters.title: The Dice Hall
chapters.subtitle: A game in which a kingdom, five brothers and a queen are staked
narrative: Duryodhana came home from Indraprastha sick with envy. His uncle Shakuni had a plan: invite Yudhishthira to a game of dice, at which Shakuni was a master. Dhritarashtra hesitated, Vidura warned that the game would destroy the family, and the blind king agreed anyway and had a new hall built. Vidura himself was sent with the invitation. Yudhishthira saw the danger, but said that he did not refuse a challenge once it was made, and he came. When Duryodhana announced that Shakuni would throw the dice on his behalf, Yudhishthira objected that one should play for oneself, then accepted.

The epic slows down for the losses. Jewels, gold, chariots, servants, the army, the kingdom. Then the brothers, beginning with Nakula and Sahadeva, then Arjuna, then Bhima. Then Yudhishthira staked himself and lost. At Shakuni's prompting he staked Draupadi, and the dice fell against him again. Vidura protested that the game was ruinous. Most of the elders said nothing.

Duryodhana sent for Draupadi as a slave. She sent back a question: had Yudhishthira lost himself before he staked her? Dushasana dragged her into the hall by her hair, in a single garment. Vikarna, a younger Kaurava, argued that she had not been lawfully won; Karna shouted him down and ordered the Pandavas and Draupadi stripped. When Dushasana pulled at her garment, the text says more cloth kept appearing. The Critical Edition records this wonder without Draupadi's prayer to Krishna, which belongs to many other manuscripts and to most popular retellings. Bhima swore terrible vows against Dushasana and Duryodhana.

Jackals howled in the king's fire-sanctuary. Alarmed, and pressed by Gandhari and Vidura, Dhritarashtra offered Draupadi boons. She asked for Yudhishthira's freedom and then for the other four brothers with their weapons, and declined a third boon. The Pandavas left free. But Duryodhana persuaded his father to call them back for one more game, with a new stake: twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year in hiding. Yudhishthira returned, played and lost.

story_context.when: The climax of the Sabha Parva, soon after the Rajasuya.

chapters.title: Draupadi's Question
chapters.subtitle: A question of law asked in a hall that had forgotten it
narrative: When the usher came to fetch her as a slave, Draupadi did not come. She sent him back with a question for the assembly: whom had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? If a man had already become another's property, what right did he have left to stake his wife? Duryodhana's answer was to send Dushasana, who dragged her into the hall by her hair, in a single garment, while she was in her monthly seclusion.

Standing before the elders, she asked again. Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was subtle, that a man without property could not stake what was not his, yet a wife remains subject to her husband, and that he could not decide. Vikarna, one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, argued that the wager was invalid: Yudhishthira had played in the grip of gambling, one of the recognised vices of kings; Draupadi was the wife of all five brothers, not his alone; he had staked her after losing himself; and Shakuni, not he, had first named her. Karna shouted him down, called Draupadi a woman with many husbands, and ordered the Pandavas and Draupadi stripped.

As Dushasana pulled at her garment, the text says that more cloth of the same kind kept appearing, until he sat down exhausted. Who protected her depends on the manuscript: the Critical Edition names no rescuer, while many other manuscripts and nearly all popular and devotional retellings have Draupadi call on Krishna, who answers. Bhima made his vows. Then omens filled the hall, and the blind king, afraid at last, offered Draupadi boons. Her question was never answered.

story_context.sources_note: The Critical Edition keeps the multiplying garment but omits Draupadi's prayer to Krishna and his intervention, which are found in many Northern and Southern manuscripts and dominate later devotional tradition. Bhishma's reply is often summarised as 'dharma is subtle'; the full answer is longer and is paraphrased here.

central_question.question: Can a man who has already lost himself still stake another?
central_question.deeper_context: Draupadi's legal question turns on whether a man who had become a slave still owned anything, including any claim over his wife. The epic lets Bhishma admit he cannot answer: one of its most deliberate silences.

questions.question: When Bhishma says the way of dharma is subtle, is that wisdom or evasion?
questions.deeper_context: Bhishma, the epic's model of integrity, tells Draupadi that dharma is subtle and that he cannot settle her question. Readers have defended this as honesty about a genuinely hard case, and condemned it as the failure of power to protect the vulnerable.

chapters.title: The Exile
chapters.subtitle: Twelve years in the forest, and what kingship could not teach
narrative: Vidura described the departure to the blind king: Yudhishthira walking with his face covered, Bhima looking at his own arms, Arjuna scattering sand, the twins smeared with dust, Draupadi weeping with her hair unbound, and the family priest Dhaumya chanting hymns for the dead. Kunti stayed behind in Vidura's house. Brahmins followed the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira, unable to feed them, prayed to the Sun, who in the epic gives him a vessel that provides food each day. Retellings describe the vessel and its rules in different ways.

In the Kamyaka and Dwaita forests the Pandavas learned what it was to have nothing to command. Bhima killed the rakshasa Kirmira. Krishna came, and Draupadi poured out her grief to him. She and Bhima pressed Yudhishthira hard: a king who forgives every wrong, they argued, abandons his duty; Draupadi went so far as to question the justice of the creator. Yudhishthira answered with a defence of patience and of keeping his word, and the epic gives both sides their full say. On Vyasa's advice Arjuna went alone to the Himalaya, fought a mysterious hunter who turned out to be Shiva, received the Pashupata weapon, and spent years in Indra's heaven learning the use of divine arms.

The forest was full of stories. The sage Brihadashva told Yudhishthira of Nala, another king who lost his kingdom at dice; Markandeya told of Rama's exile and of Savitri, who argued with Death for her husband's life. The brothers went on pilgrimage to sacred fords, and on a mountain path Bhima met Hanuman, his elder brother as a fellow son of the Wind. These embedded tales make up a large share of the Vana Parva, and they seem chosen to show the exiles their own situation from the outside.

Enemies did not leave them alone. Duryodhana came to the forest to show off his wealth, was captured by Gandharvas, and was freed by the Pandavas at Yudhishthira's insistence, a rescue more humiliating to him than defeat. Jayadratha tried to carry off Draupadi and was caught and spared. And Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, asked Karna for his natural armour and earrings, and Karna gave them.

chapters.title: The Yaksha's Questions
chapters.subtitle: A still lake, a voice and a final choice
narrative: Near the end of the forest years, a Brahmin came to the Pandavas in distress: a deer had carried off his fire-sticks on its antlers. The brothers gave chase deep into the Dwaita forest until thirst overcame them. Nakula climbed a tree, saw water, and went to fetch it. At the lake a voice, seemingly from a crane, told him to answer its questions before drinking. He drank and fell. Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima followed him, ignored the voice, and fell beside the water.

Yudhishthira came last and found his brothers lying still. He did not drink. He asked who spoke, and a towering Yaksha showed himself and put his questions: about the sun and the earth, about dharma, happiness, the path to follow and the nature of a person. Yudhishthira answered each in turn. Among the answers best remembered: a mother outweighs the earth and a father stands higher than the sky; and the greatest wonder is that every day people watch others die, yet those who remain live as if they never will.

Then the Yaksha offered to restore one brother. Yudhishthira passed over Bhima and Arjuna, the warriors he would need, and chose Nakula, so that Madri, like Kunti, would still have a living son. The Yaksha revealed himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's divine father, restored all four, returned the fire-sticks and granted that the Pandavas would pass their thirteenth year unrecognised. The number, wording and order of the questions vary between manuscripts, and popular collections often add more.

story_context.sources_note: The Yaksha Prashna is in the Critical Edition, but the number, wording and order of the questions differ between manuscripts; popular lists often contain questions not found in the Critical Edition. The answers quoted in summaries are paraphrases.

central_question.question: What makes a question a test of character rather than of knowledge?
central_question.deeper_context: Four brothers ignored the voice and drank; Yudhishthira listened and answered. The Yaksha's final test was not a riddle at all but a choice: which brother should live.
